claims.text: A homogeneous single-phase HEA coating serves as the initial material state and monolithic baseline.
Interfaces between alternating HEA layers act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Slight compositional or structural differences between layers generate coherency strains and local lattice distortions.
Coherency strains and local lattice distortions pin dislocations.
Interfacial dislocation pinning reduces both dislocation glide and climb under sustained load.
Depositing alternating HEA layers with varied compositions or crystal structures can produce coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
The relevant structural mediator is an interfacial region with mismatched lattice parameters and a locally altered microstructure.
HEAs can undergo elevated-temperature mechanical deformation and creep testing.
Interfacial regions impede deformation in a manner analogous to precipitation hardening.
Monolithic coatings lack the layer interfaces proposed to impede dislocations.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have lower creep rates than identically processed monolithic HEA coatings under equivalent temperature and stress.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have longer times to failure than monolithic HEA coatings under equivalent creep conditions.
The proposed interfacial advantage should be most significant at elevated temperatures where creep is prominent.
The interfacial advantage may be less observable at low temperatures because dislocation mobility is inherently reduced.
The magnitude of creep-resistance improvement depends on layer composition, individual layer thickness, and interfacial bonding quality.
In situ neutron diffraction can be used to follow deformation and microstructural evolution during elevated-temperature mechanical testing of an HEA.
Creep strain rate, time to failure, and dislocation distributions near interfaces are measurable outcomes for the proposed comparison.
Failure to observe either a significantly lower creep rate or an extended time to failure in the multilayer coating would falsify the proposed dominant interfacial-pinning mechanism.
